The wind didn’t just blow on the jagged cliffs of Blackwood Point; it screamed. It was a high, thin shriek that had been the only companion for Arthur Penhaligon for the last three decades. To the world below, the lighthouse was a beacon of safety, a rhythmic pulse cutting through the fog. To Arthur, it was a solitary cell, a tower of stone and salt where the horizon was the only view worth having.

Arthur’s hands, mapped with the topography of his long life, were busy scrubbing the salt crust from the brass railing. He was old, his hair white as the foam that crashed against the rocks hundreds of feet below. He had forgotten the sound of a human voice that wasn’t the creaking of the door or the groan of the sea. He had forgotten the warmth of a hand that wasn’t his own.

It was a Tuesday, grey and heavy with rain, when he found it.

He had been checking the perimeter for debris, a mundane task he performed with the mechanical precision of a metronome. There, wedged tight between two jagged rocks near the base of the stairs, sat a bottle. It was thick glass, green as deep water, and uncorked. The cork was swollen, dark with age.

Arthur hesitated. In his thirty years, he had seen a thousand bottles wash ashore. Most were empty, or filled with sand, or contained the dry bones of long-forgotten sailors. But this one felt heavy. It felt *intentional*.

With trembling fingers, he pried the cork loose. The smell that escaped was not of rot or stale beer, but of lavender and old paper. Inside was a single, rolled-up piece of parchment, yellowed but intact.

He unfolded it on the railing, the wind trying to snatch it from him. The handwriting was elegant, looping, and unmistakably feminine.

*"If you have found this, know that I am gone. The sea took my husband, and then it took my will to stay. I am leaving everything behind, but I am leaving this note to say: Look up. The stars are still there, even when the fog is thick. Don’t let the grey swallow you whole. Live, Arthur. Or whoever you are. Live."*

Arthur stared at the name. His breath caught in his throat. It was his own name. But the handwriting wasn’t his. It was the handwriting of Eleanor,

He was old, his hair white as the foam that crashed against the rocks hundreds of feet below. He had forgotten the sound of a human voice that wasn’t the creaking of the door or the groan of the sea. He had forgotten the warmth of a hand that wasn’t his own.

It was a Tuesday, grey and heavy with rain, when he found it.

He had been checking the perimeter for debris, a mundane task he performed with the mechanical precision of a metronome. There, wedged tight between two jagged rocks near the base of the stairs, sat a bottle. It was thick glass, green as deep water, and uncorked. The cork was swollen, dark with age.

Arthur hesitated. In his thirty years, he had seen a thousand bottles wash ashore. Most were empty, or filled with sand, or contained the dry bones of long-forgotten sailors. But this one felt heavy. It felt *intentional*.

With trembling fingers, he pried the cork loose. The smell that escaped was not of rot or stale beer, but of lavender and old paper. Inside was a single, rolled-up piece of parchment, yellowed but intact.

He unfolded it on the railing, the wind trying to snatch it from him. The handwriting was elegant, looping, and unmistakably feminine.

*"If you have found this, know that I am gone. The sea took my husband, and then it took my will to stay. I am leaving everything behind, but I am leaving this note to say: Look up. The stars are still there, even when the fog is thick. Don’t let the grey swallow you whole. Live, Arthur. Or whoever you are. Live."*
